interest: This file offers valuable insight into Japan's cultural diplomacy and soft power strategies in the late 1930s, specifically its efforts to cultivate ties with Central European states such as Hungary following the Anti-Comintern Pact. Baron Takaharu Mitsui's explicit commentary underscores how Japanese elites viewed cultural and spiritual outreach in Central Europe as an ideological buffer against the Soviet Union. In addition, the 1934 memoranda illustrate State Department cross-referencing and inter-divisional coordination (between Far Eastern Affairs, Latin American Affairs, and Research and Publication) in verifying the private, unofficial nature of cultural and library initiatives.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.42764) relates to Japanese cultural relations, international educational ties, and library initiatives between 1934 and 1938. The primary 1938 documentation consists of reporting from the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo regarding the imminent conclusion of a Japan-Hungarian cultural pact, an annual Japan-Cultural Prize established by the Japan-Hungarian Cultural Society under Baron Takaharu Mitsui, and Mitsui's multi-year financial campaign to foster pro-Japanese sentiment in Central Europe as an ideological counterweight to Soviet Russia. The file also contains 1934 internal State Department memoranda from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs and the Division of Research and Publication investigating statements by Herbert S. Houston concerning an alleged Pan-American or Latin American library in New York, which was determined to be a private initiative sponsored by the Pan American Society without official government connection.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 3521 regarding a forthcoming Japan-Hungarian cultural pact and cultural prize.
subfiles.summary: This Document File Note indexes Despatch No. 3521 (894.00 P.M./132) dated December 20, 1938, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo. It notes that a Japan-Hungarian cultural pact was reportedly to be concluded within a short time. It also records the announcement that an annual Japan-Cultural Prize would be instituted to commemorate the event.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Tokyo Despatch No. 3521 Regarding Japan-Hungarian Cultural Pact

subfiles.about: Diplomatic report extract concerning Japanese press reports on the Japan-Hungarian cultural pact and Baron Takaharu Mitsui's cultural endowment.
subfiles.summary: This extract reports press accounts from November 28, 1938, announcing that a Japan-Hungarian cultural pact was slated for imminent conclusion. The Japan-Hungarian Cultural Society, chaired by Baron Takaharu Mitsui, announced the creation of the annual Japan-Cultural Prize to award medals and monetary gifts to Hungarians who introduce Japanese culture. The report highlights Baron Mitsui's five-year funding program of 30,000 yen annually and quotes his view that promoting Japanese culture in Central European nations bordering Soviet Russia is essential.
subfiles.title: Despatch Extract on Japan-Hungarian Cultural Pact and Baron Mitsui's Cultural Initiatives

subfiles.about: Internal memorandum regarding the private sponsorship of the Latin American Library and Center in New York.
subfiles.summary: This internal State Department memorandum from staff member mjs in the Division of Research and Publication is addressed to Mrs. Margaret M. Hanna. Citing information provided by Mr. Babcock of the Pan American Union, it clarifies that the Latin American Library and Center at 67 Broad Street, New York, managed by Wade H. Everhart, is privately sponsored by the Pan American Society. The note affirms that the library has no official government connection and cites a reference in the August 1934 issue of the Foreign Service Journal.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Latin American Library and Center in New York

subfiles.about: Internal memorandum from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs addressing Herbert S. Houston's statement regarding a Pan-American Library in New York.
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs notes an attached letter of August 6, 1934, from Herbert S. Houston asserting that a Pan-American Library was established in New York the preceding January. Hamilton records that Mr. McGurk of the Division of Latin American Affairs was unaware of any such official library, although the Pan-American Society of New York may have established one. McGurk confirmed that any such institution would be entirely private and unofficial in character.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Inquiries Concerning Proposed Pan-American Library in New York
